title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2025
official_title: To extend the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000.
likelihoodReason: Signed into law December 18, 2025 as Public Law 119-58. Sponsored by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID) with 28 cosponsors; passed the Senate June 18, 2025 and the House December 9, 2025.
summary: The Secure Rural Schools (SRS) program, first enacted in 2000, pays counties that contain Forest Service or Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land a formula-based "State payment" or "county payment" for schools, roads, and other municipal services — an alternative to the traditional 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) share of receipts from timber sales and other federal-land revenues. This Act reauthorizes those SRS payments through fiscal year 2026, restores the lapsed payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 (which the Secretary of the Treasury must pay within 45 days of enactment), and extends the authority to initiate Resource Advisory Committee (RAC) Title II special projects on federal land and to spend Title III county funds through fiscal year 2028.
brief: Reauthorizes the Secure Rural Schools program through fiscal year 2026, pays out the lapsed fiscal year 2024 and 2025 amounts within 45 days of enactment, and extends the Title II special-projects and Title III county-funds authorities through fiscal year 2028.

top_lines.headline: What SRS Pays For
subs: Formula payments to counties containing Forest Service or BLM land
Funds schools, roads, and other municipal services
Alternative to the 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) revenue share

top_lines.headline: SRS Payments Extended
subs: State/county payment authority extended through fiscal year 2026
Restores payments that lapsed for fiscal years 2024 and 2025
Treasury must issue those lapsed payments within 45 days of enactment

top_lines.headline: Election Waived for 2024-2025
subs: Counties skip the biennial election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025
Their fiscal year 2023 election choice carries over automatically

top_lines.headline: Title II & Title III Extensions
subs: RAC special-projects initiation authority extended from 2025 to 2028
Unobligated Title II funds return to Treasury deadline pushed from 2026 to 2029
County Title III fund-expenditure authority extended from 2025 to 2028
RAC composition waiver and pilot program authorities extended to 2026

sections.label: Section 2 — Extension of Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000

items.main: Extends the SRS State and county payment authority in Section 101 (16 U.S.C. 7111) and the California-only county-share distribution rule in Section 103(d)(2) (16 U.S.C. 7113(d)(2)) by striking "2023" and inserting "2026" wherever those year references appear.
items.detail: Section 101 sets the formula the Secretary of Agriculture and Secretary of the Interior use to calculate the State payment (Forest Service counties) and county payment (BLM counties) for eligible jurisdictions. Section 103(d) is a California-only rule that distributes the State-payment share to California's eligible counties in the same proportion those counties received under the pre-2008 formula. The prior authorization covered fiscal years 2008-2015 and 2017-2023; the extension adds fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026.

items.main: Adds a new Section 101(e) with a special rule for fiscal year 2024 and 2025 payments and a 45-day prompt-payment deadline for the Secretary of the Treasury.
items.detail: For any eligible county that already received a share of the 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) payment for fiscal year 2024 or 2025, the corresponding State or county payment is reduced by the amount already received — preventing double payment. The Secretary of the Treasury must make all title I payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 not later than 45 days after enactment.

items.main: Amends Section 102 (16 U.S.C. 7112) so counties do not have to file a fresh biennial election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 — their fiscal year 2023 election choice carries over.
items.detail: Under existing law each affected county elects between the 25-percent/50-percent traditional payment and the State/county SRS payment on a two-fiscal-year cycle. The bill waives that election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 for both the payment-type choice in subsection (b) and the intended use-of-funds choice in subsection (d), with the fiscal year 2023 elections treated as effective for those years.

items.main: Extends the Title II authority to initiate special projects on federal land under Section 208 (16 U.S.C. 7128) from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2028, and pushes the deadline for depositing unobligated project funds in the Treasury from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2029.
items.detail: Title II projects — proposed by Resource Advisory Committees for forest restoration, road maintenance, watershed work, and similar activities on Forest Service and BLM land — could no longer be initiated after September 30, 2025 under prior law. The bill gives RACs three more fiscal years to obligate project funds and three more years before unspent balances revert.

items.main: Extends the Title III authority for eligible counties to expend county funds under Section 305 (16 U.S.C. 7144) from 2025 to 2028, and the corresponding return-of-funds deadline from 2026 to 2029.
items.detail: Title III funds are the portion of the SRS payment a county may spend directly on carrying out the Firewise Communities program, reimbursing emergency services on federal land, or developing community wildfire protection plans. The bill extends both the authority to spend and the deadline to obligate by three fiscal years.

sections.label: Section 3 — Resource Advisory Committee Pilot Program Extension

items.main: Extends the Resource Advisory Committee pilot program in Section 205(g) (16 U.S.C. 7125(g)) from 2023 to 2026 by striking "2023" in the paragraph (5) termination-of-effectiveness clause, and strikes paragraph (6) (the post-termination "Report to Congress" requirement).
items.detail: Paragraph (5) is the pilot program's actual sunset — before this bill it terminated on October 1, 2023. Paragraph (6) required the Secretary to report back to Congress within 180 days of that termination date on how regional vs. national appointments compared. Extending paragraph (5)'s date to 2026 keeps the pilot running through fiscal year 2026, and striking paragraph (6) removes the accompanying report-to-Congress requirement.

items.main: Makes technical corrections to Section 205 (16 U.S.C. 7125) and Section 206(b)(2) (16 U.S.C. 7126(b)(2)) — punctuation, a missing article, and replacing "the date of the enactment of this Act" with the fixed date "October 3, 2008".
items.detail: The corrections replace "concerned," with "concerned" in two places (Section 205(c)(1) and Section 206(b)(2)), insert "the" into the phrase "to extent", and fix the ambiguous cross-reference to an enactment date by naming the specific date the underlying provisions took effect.

underreported.summary: The Secretary of the Treasury has 45 days after enactment to issue every fiscal year 2024 and 2025 SRS payment — a fixed deliverable placed inside the retroactive-payment offset rules.
underreported.why_unreported: The 45-day Treasury deadline sits inside a subsection captioned "Special Rule for Fiscal Year 2024 and 2025 Payments," whose text is otherwise devoted to double-payment offsets — the operational deliverable is not surfaced in the section heading.

underreported.section: Section 3 — Resource Advisory Committee Pilot Program Extension
underreported.summary: Along with extending the pilot, the section strikes paragraph (6) of 16 U.S.C. 7125(g) entirely — a removal, not just an extension.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label describes only the extension; the removal of paragraph (6) is not signaled in the section title.

gaps: The bill extends SRS payments through fiscal year 2026 but does not appropriate a specific dollar amount — the payment formula in 16 U.S.C. 7111 relies on the "full funding amount" defined elsewhere in the underlying Act, and no new authorization figure is stated.

The bill provides retroactive fiscal year 2024 and 2025 payments but does not address whether counties owe interest, penalty offsets, or reconciliation for spending decisions already made on the assumption no payment would arrive.
The bill extends Title II special-projects authority to fiscal year 2028 but does not add or modify criteria for which projects a Resource Advisory Committee may recommend.
The bill relies on the existing 25-percent and 50-percent revenue-sharing baselines but does not adjust those percentages to reflect current federal-land receipt levels.

The bill covers Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management counties but does not extend SRS eligibility to counties containing other categories of federal land (e.g., National Park Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs, military installations).

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Salinas
featured_quotes.text: In central and southern Oregon, my district, the Federal Government owns over 3 million acres of forestland that pays no taxes to our local government. Generations of families built their lives and livelihood around Federal timber harvest, and counties relied on revenue shares from those sales to fund public services. When the timber industry collapsed, the revenue shares also disappeared. Congress made a commitment to support rural communities and the critical infrastructure to make sure they did not get left behind.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Lamalfa
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate being able to get this over the line here soon, as we both know too much about wildfires in our respective States, as well. This will go a long way toward helping that issue.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bentz
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, in 1990, the spotted owl was listed under the Endangered Species Act as a threatened species. Almost immediately, timber production from Federal forests in the Western United States plummeted by 80 percent. The economic and societal costs of timber-dependent States and their timber-reliant counties was appalling. Demand for SNAP and Medicaid shot up. Alcoholism and meth addictions became routine. County tax revenues were decimated.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, with such a large percentage of Wyoming's resources historically locked up in Federal lands, including national forests, communities across my State have long weathered challenges associated with reduced flexibility and a decreased tax base. While a percentage of revenue from timber sales previously alleviated tax shortfalls, shifting land management priorities in Washington, D.C., have led to significant declines in timber harvest.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: This bill is vital to restoring critical funding, preventing further school closures, and ensuring rural students have access to quality education that can compete with urban communities. However, this is not just an education issue. This is about investing in the future of rural America and supporting communities surrounded by Federal forests.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Actively managing our national forests is critical for both forest health and the economic health of our rural communities. Congress has long recognized that responsible timber harvesting is essential for encouraging that stewardship. Since many communities throughout the United States, including Pennsylvania's 15th Congressional District, are located within national forest lands, declining timber harvests can lead to chronic underfunding of local schools, emergency services, and other projects that rely on a strong tax base.

16 U.S.C. 7125(d)(6)(C) (RAC committee composition waiver authority) — year "2023" replaced with "2026"
